title: Hooks and managed settings for people

story: Tuesday afternoon. A new engineer is connecting the frontend to a test storage bucket, and to get it working quickly he asks Claude to put the AWS access key straight into src/config.ts. Claude writes the file, he commits, and the push goes out. The secret scanner finds the key twenty minutes later, someone rotates it, and the afternoon is gone.

rhino-core, the plugin every engineer is supposed to have, carries a hook that refuses exactly this write. It would have stopped him. But he joined last month and nobody told him to install it, and on the laptop next to his, a colleague turned rhino-core off because the lint check felt slow.
hook.question: How do we put a safety hook on every laptop, and keep it there, without asking each person?

read.h: A hook in a plugin is a small program
p: In the lesson about hooks in the Agent SDK, you wrote hooks as TypeScript functions inside Nova's harness. Claude Code on a laptop runs the same idea as a command. A plugin declares its hooks in hooks/hooks.json: the event (PreToolUse runs before a tool call), a matcher with the tool names (Write|Edit), and the command to run. Before every matching call, Claude Code starts the command and sends it the call as JSON on stdin, with fields such as tool_name and tool_input.

The command answers with its exit code. Exit 0 lets the call go ahead. Exit 2 blocks it, and whatever the script printed on stderr goes back to Claude as the reason, so a good message says what to do instead. Any other exit code is treated as a non-blocking error: Claude Code shows a notice and the call goes ahead. That last rule matters for a guard, because a guard that crashes does not block anything.

rhino-core's guard is written in Python with only the standard library, while the rest of our platform is TypeScript. The reason is practical: a hook runs straight from the plugin folder on every laptop with no install step, and python3 comes with Apple's command line tools on every Mac, while Node does not.

code.file: plugins/guard/hooks/guard_write.py (the lab version of rhino-core's guard)
code.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PreToolUse hook: refuse a Write or Edit that holds a secret or touches a credential file."""
import json
import re
import sys

SECRET = re.compile(r"AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|gh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}|xox[baprs]-[A-Za-z0-9-]{10,}|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----")
CREDENTIAL_FILE = re.compile(r"(^|/)(\.env[^/]*|[^/]+\.pem|id_rsa[^/]*)$|(^|/)secrets/")

event = json.load(sys.stdin)
args = event.get("tool_input", {})
path = args.get("file_path", "")
text = args.get("content", "") + args.get("new_string", "")

if CREDENTIAL_FILE.search(path):
    print(f"{path} looks like a credential file. Keep secrets out of the repo; read them from the environment.", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(2)
if SECRET.search(text):
    print("This text looks like a secret (an access key, a token or a private key). Use an environment variable instead.", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(2)
sys.exit(0)

notes.text: Shapes of real secrets: an AWS key id, GitHub tokens, Slack tokens and private key blocks.
Paths that hold credentials: .env files, .pem files, SSH keys and any secrets/ folder.
The tool call arrives as JSON on stdin.
Write sends content and Edit sends new_string. .get with a default keeps the guard from crashing on either tool.
Exit 2 blocks the call. The stderr line just above becomes Claude's reason.
Exit 0: nothing found, the write goes ahead.

read.h: Five layers of settings, and one on top
p: A hook only helps on a machine where its plugin is enabled, and that is decided by settings. Claude Code reads settings from several layers. Your own ~/.claude/settings.json applies to every project. A repo's .claude/settings.json is shared with everyone who opens the repo, and .claude/settings.local.json is yours inside one project. A --settings flag changes one session. When two layers set the same key, the higher layer wins, except for lists such as permission rules, which are combined.

Above all of them sits one more layer, managed settings, which an administrator deploys. Nothing below it can override a key it sets: not your user settings, not the project, not a command-line flag. That is the tool for the Tuesday problem. If managed settings say rhino-core is enabled, the plugin is installed at the start of the next session, and a person who sets it to false in their own file simply has no effect.

code.text:
managed settings              set by an admin; nothing below can override a key here
  --settings <file-or-json>   one session, from the command line
    .claude/settings.local.json   you, in this project (not committed)
      .claude/settings.json       everyone in this project (committed)
        ~/.claude/settings.json     you, in every project

~/.claude/settings.json on the new engineer's laptop:
{ "enabledPlugins": { "rhino-core@rhino": false } }

managed settings:
{ "enabledPlugins": { "rhino-core@rhino": true } }      <- this one wins

notes.text: The policy layer. An admin writes it; a person on the laptop cannot change what it says.
The lowest layer: your personal settings.
The colleague's attempt to switch rhino-core off.
Managed settings set the same key, so the plugin stays on.

read.h: How the policy reaches a laptop
p: Managed settings can arrive in three ways. Server-managed settings are typed into the claude.ai admin console by an organization Owner, and Claude Code fetches them at startup and then every hour. An MDM profile (pushed by a device-management tool) carries the same keys. The simplest is a file: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json on a Mac, /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json on Linux. By default only one of the three applies on a machine, the first one found in that order.

Next to the file, a folder called managed-settings.d holds drop-ins: separate *.json files that are merged in alphabetical order, which is why they get number prefixes. Each team can own one file instead of everyone editing one shared document. When two drop-ins set the same key, a single value from the later file replaces the earlier one, two lists are combined, and two objects are merged key by key. Inside Claude Code, /status shows a Setting sources line that names the managed source in use, for example Enterprise managed settings (file).

The drop-in that answers the Tuesday problem does two things. extraKnownMarketplaces registers our marketplace on every machine, and enabledPlugins forces rhino-core on. A third key, strictKnownMarketplaces, limits where anyone may add marketplaces from at all.

notes.text: Marketplaces may come only from repos under RhinoHealth. The /* wildcard works only in this key.
Any allow-list also stops plugins in ~/.claude/skills from loading; this entry keeps them.
Register the rhino marketplace on every machine, at the stable branch.
Keep the marketplace and its plugins up to date in the background.
Force rhino-core on. In managed settings, false would block it everywhere instead.

deeper.h: Go deeper: agents and API keys
p: Server-managed settings reach a session only when it signs in to the same claude.ai organization. A session that signs in with an API key from the Claude Console belongs to a different organization, so it never receives them. Agent machines and CI jobs usually run that way, which is why they get the policy as a file in the machine image instead.

If one machine receives the policy from two places, Claude Code by default uses the highest one (server, then MDM, then file) and ignores the rest, with no warning except in /status. Setting managedSourcesBehavior to "merge" makes it combine them instead.

read.h: Only the MCP servers we approved
p: Plugins are not the only thing a laptop loads. MCP servers can come from a person's own settings, from a plugin, from a --mcp-config flag, and from claude.ai connectors such as Jira or Slack, which Claude Code fetches by itself. One of our MCP servers reaches a database with test data, and the same server in production reaches customer data. Patient data must never enter a prompt, so the production one must never load on a laptop, whoever adds it.

Two managed keys do this. allowedMcpServers is the list of servers that may load, here matched by URL. allowManagedMcpServersOnly makes the managed list the only one that counts, so a server someone adds to their own settings is ignored unless the policy lists it too. Because the list also blocks claude.ai connectors, a rollout starts with an inventory of what people use every day; otherwise the policy quietly takes their Jira and Slack tools away.

notes.text: Only the managed list counts. Lists in user, project and local settings are ignored.
Matched by URL with * wildcards. The test-data server is allowed; production is simply not listed.

lab.title: A guard on every laptop
needs: Claude Code 2.1.269 or later, for claude plugin validate
No admin rights: the policy part uses a small model of the documented rules
lab.goal: Build a guard hook, prove what it blocks, and write managed-settings drop-ins that force it on and limit MCP servers, then watch a laptop's own settings fail to override them.

guess.q: Managed settings force rhino-core on. On her laptop, a colleague writes "rhino-core@rhino": false in ~/.claude/settings.json. What happens at her next session?

options.text: rhino-core is off, because her own file decides what runs on her laptop.
options.why: User settings are the lowest layer. A key set in managed settings cannot be overridden from below.

options.text: Claude Code refuses to start until the two files agree.
options.why: There is nothing to resolve: the higher layer wins, and Claude Code starts normally.

options.text: rhino-core stays on, because managed settings sit above every other layer.
options.why: That is the point of the policy layer: what it sets, nobody on the laptop can undo.

follow.say: Make a lab folder and write a small plugin whose only job is the guard hook. The script is the same one the lesson explains.
A hook is just a program that reads one tool call from stdin, so you can test it without Claude. Write four fake tool calls, the shape Claude Code sends.
follow.do:
mkdir -p events
printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Write","tool_input":{"file_path":"src/config.ts","content":"export const key = \"AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE\";"}}' > events/write-key.json
printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Edit","tool_input":{"file_path":"src/aws.ts","old_string":"KEY = \"\"","new_string":"KEY = \"AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE\""}}' > events/edit-key.json
printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Edit","tool_input":{"file_path":"frontend/.env.local","old_string":"A=1","new_string":"A=2"}}' > events/edit-env.json
printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Write","tool_input":{"file_path":"src/config.ts","content":"export const region = \"eu-west-1\";"}}' > events/write-region.json
ls events

follow.say: Feed each call to the guard and print its exit code, because the exit code is the hook's whole answer: 2 blocks, 0 lets the call through.
follow.do: for e in events/*.json; do echo "$e:"; python3 plugins/guard/hooks/guard_write.py < "$e"; echo "  exit $?"; done
follow.see:
events/edit-env.json:
frontend/.env.local looks like a credential file. Keep secrets out of the repo; read them from the environment.
  exit 2
events/edit-key.json:
This text looks like a secret (an access key, a token or a private key). Use an environment variable instead.
  exit 2
…
events/write-region.json:
  exit 0

follow.say: Now the policy. Write four drop-ins, the way four teams would each own one file, and the settings file of the laptop that tried to switch rhino-core off.
Changing the real managed settings needs admin rights, so run a small model of the two documented rules instead: drop-ins merge in name order, and the policy sits above the laptop.
follow.see:
drop-ins merged in this order: 10-models.json, 20-telemetry.json, 30-plugins.json, 40-mcp.json
rhino-core@rhino enabled: true
MCP servers allowed: https://mcp-dev3.example.com/*
OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS: 0
denied models: fable

follow.say: Guess first, then try it: delete the line "allowManagedMcpServersOnly": true from 40-mcp.json and run the model again. Put the line back afterwards.

lab.build: Your inventory found that people use the Jira connector every day. Add a fifth drop-in, policy/managed-settings.d/45-connectors.json, that allows https://mcp.atlassian.com/* without touching 40-mcp.json, and run node effective.mjs: both servers are allowed, because lists from different drop-ins are combined. Then put the same entry only in laptop/settings.json instead and run it again: it is ignored, because allowManagedMcpServersOnly makes the managed list the only one that counts. Finally, on your real laptop, open Claude Code, type /status and read the Setting sources line: it says whether a managed policy reaches your machine today, and from where.
checks: The guard exits 2 with a readable reason for write-key, edit-key and edit-env, and exits 0 for write-region.
claude plugin validate plugins/guard --strict prints Validation passed.
node effective.mjs shows rhino-core@rhino enabled: true, although laptop/settings.json says false.
Without allowManagedMcpServersOnly the production server from the laptop appears in the allowed list; with it, it does not.
With 45-connectors.json in place, both the dev3 server and the Atlassian server are allowed.
lab.fix: Someone made the guard "simpler" by changing one line to text = args["content"] + args.get("new_string", ""). Their test with write-key still exits 2, so they merged it. Run the changed guard with events/edit-key.json: Python stops with KeyError: 'content' and exit code 1. Exit 1 is a non-blocking error, so in Claude Code that Edit, which puts an AWS key into src/aws.ts, would go ahead. Find why Edit calls crash the guard and put back the safe version.
explain: What do exit codes 0, 2 and 1 each mean to Claude Code, and why is a crashing guard dangerous?
A colleague turns rhino-core off in ~/.claude/settings.json, but managed settings force it on. Which wins, and why?
Why does the MCP allow-list rollout start with an inventory of the connectors people use?
lab.done: The guard blocks the three bad calls and allows the harmless one, the model shows rhino-core on despite the laptop, and you can explain why the crashing guard let a key through.

check.q: A guard hook crashes with a Python error (exit code 1) on an Edit that adds an AWS key. What does Claude Code do with the Edit?

options.text: Blocks it, because any error in a PreToolUse hook blocks the call
options.why: Only exit code 2 blocks. Other codes are treated as a non-blocking error.

options.text: Asks the user whether to continue
options.why: A crash does not turn into a question. Asking is a separate decision a hook can return on purpose.

options.text: Shows a hook error notice and lets the Edit go ahead
options.why: A non-2 failure does not stop the call. That is why a guard must never crash on the tools it guards.

check.q: Security wants the production MCP server never to load on a laptop, even if someone adds it to their own settings. What does that take?

options.text: allowManagedMcpServersOnly: true and an allowedMcpServers list without the production server, in managed settings
options.why: The managed list becomes the only list that counts, and production is not on it.

options.text: An allowedMcpServers list in the repo's .claude/settings.json
options.why: A project file sits below managed settings, and without the lock, allow-lists from every file are combined, so a person's own list can still add the production server.

options.text: A sentence in rhino-core's skills asking Claude not to use that server
options.why: A sentence is guidance, not a wall. The model can be wrong or tricked; the allow-list cannot.

check.q: Why does turning on the MCP allow-list start with an inventory of five laptops?

options.text: Claude Code needs the inventory to download the servers
options.why: The inventory is for people. Claude Code never reads it.

options.text: The allow-list also blocks claude.ai connectors, so anything people use daily must be on the list first
options.why: Without the inventory, the policy would quietly take away Jira, Slack or Figma tools.

options.text: Each laptop needs its own allow-list
options.why: There is one policy for everyone; the inventory feeds that one list.

p: Our policy is one set of drop-ins kept in RhinoHealth/ai-agents under settings/managed-settings.d/, so every change is a reviewed pull request. 10-models.json blocks Fable models and keeps agent teams off, 20-telemetry.json turns on telemetry with prompt and tool content off, and the plugin rollout adds the marketplace, rhino-core and MCP keys. Platform is the single writer of the policy, because three projects add keys to it. People receive it through the claude.ai admin console or a Fleet MDM profile (still to decide with DevOps and Security); agent VMs get the same files in /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.d/ through the machine image, because their sessions sign in with a Console API key.

rhino-core carries two hooks: the guard you built, and a PostToolUse lint hook that runs Biome on an edited frontend file or black, isort and flake8 on backend Python, and reports problems without blocking. Because a hook, a script or an MCP config in a plugin runs code on every machine, plugin CI labels any pull request that changes them as high risk, and the one reviewer runs the plugin locally before approving. A new MCP server also needs Security and an entry in the allow-list, so a skill that runs a CLI is preferred.

tickets.why: rhino-core's hooks: refuse secrets and credential files before a write, lint the file after an edit.
The rollout: our marketplaces only, rhino-core forced on, an MCP allow-list by URL, a pilot on 3 people first.
Plugin CI: gitleaks, and a high-risk label on changes to hooks, scripts, MCP config or allowed-tools.
The first managed-settings drop-in (Fable blocked, agent teams off) and the file copy for agent VMs.

words.plain: A hook that runs a program: the tool call arrives as JSON on stdin, exit 2 blocks it, any other failure lets it through.
The settings layer an administrator deploys. No user, project or command-line setting can override a key it sets.
The order in which settings layers win: managed, command line, project local, project, user.
One *.json file in managed-settings.d/. The files merge in alphabetical order, so each team can own one.
allowedMcpServers with allowManagedMcpServersOnly: only the servers the policy lists may load, claude.ai connectors included.

review.q: Write the managed-settings keys that register a marketplace called rhino from RhinoHealth/claude-plugins at the stable branch and force rhino-core on.
review.a: extraKnownMarketplaces with rhino → source github, repo RhinoHealth/claude-plugins, ref stable (autoUpdate true), and enabledPlugins { "rhino-core@rhino": true }.

review.q: Your guard must handle a new tool that sends its text in a field called body. What do you change, and how do you prove it still never crashes?
review.a: Read the new field with .get and a default, add it to the text you scan, and feed the guard fake events for every tool, checking exit 2 for a secret and 0 for clean text, never 1.

remember: A hook guards only the machines it runs on, and managed settings are how you make sure it runs on all of them.
